strengths: Novel problem formulation: Accountability attribution for training stages is a well-motivated, timely problem that complements existing data-centric attribution methods
Principled theoretical framework: Sound application of potential outcomes formalism with formal error bounds (Theorem 4.1) characterizing when the method is reliable
Accounts for optimization dynamics: Unlike prior data attribution work, incorporates learning rate schedules, momentum, and weight decay
Efficient computational design: Stage embeddings decouple training dynamics from test instances, enabling reusable computations
Strong validation on some benchmarks: High correlations with retraining ground truth on MNIST (0.9456) and CivilComments (0.86-0.98) demonstrate estimator accuracy
Practical demonstrations: Shows utility for spurious correlation detection and identifying beneficial/harmful stages
Transparent limitations discussion: §6.1 honestly acknowledges practical constraints and fundamental challenges
weaknesses: Variable experimental validation with concerning patterns: Correlations with retraining vary dramatically (0.55-0.99), with notably low Stage 1 correlations on CELEBA (0.55) and Stage 3 on X-ray (0.74). No analysis of why these fail, limiting practical trustworthiness

Severe scalability limitations: Experiments only on small-to-medium models (MLPs, ResNet-18). No foundation model experiments despite their increasing importance. Computational complexity O(K|B|p²) even with efficiency gains

First-order approximation breaks down for early interventions: Error bound grows exponentially in K-t₁, suggesting unreliability for early stages. Empirical characterization of when this occurs missing

Restrictive practical requirements: Requires complete training logs (unrealistic in distributed settings, checkpoint-only scenarios); GGN Hessian approximation unvalidated; limited to SGD with momentum (not Adam/modern optimizers)

Insufficient experimental rigor: No simpler baselines for comparison, no ablation studies on design choices (GGN impact, layer-wise approximation accuracy, interpolation parameter sensitivity), no wall-clock time/memory reporting

Gap between problem scope and experimental capability: Accountability attribution most valuable for large models where method's limitations are most severe; experiments only demonstrate small-model performance
Missing generalization analysis: Unclear sensitivity to batch ordering, architecture changes, non-convex loss landscape regions; spectral bound assumption on propagators not empirically validated

strengths: Novel problem formulation that addresses an important gap in AI accountability by tracing model behavior to specific training stages rather than just data points

Rigorous theoretical framework based on potential outcomes with principled error bounds (Theorem 4.1) showing how approximation error depends on intervention magnitude, landscape curvature, and training stability
Distinguishes from prior work by accounting for both data AND optimization dynamics (learning rates, momentum, weight decay), with stage embeddings enabling efficient reuse without retraining
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (vision and language) with ground truth comparisons via retraining, achieving high correlations on MNIST (0.9456 average)
Demonstrates practical applications including spurious correlation detection, mislabeled data identification, and understanding domain generalization effects
Honest and thorough discussion of limitations (first-order approximation, scalability, requirements for complete training history)
weaknesses: Experimental results on complex datasets show concerning accuracy degradation: CelebA Stage 1 (0.5524 correlation) and X-Ray Stage 3 (0.7414) are substantially lower than MNIST results, with no analysis of why or when the method is reliable

First-order approximation error grows exponentially with time remaining in training (e^(2ηΛ(K-t₁))), potentially making early-stage interventions fundamentally unreliable, yet empirical validation of this error growth is absent
Hessian approximation using GGN introduces additional errors not incorporated in Theorem 4.1, with no ablation studies or empirical validation of this critical design choice

Limited algorithmic novelty—the core technique (first-order Taylor expansion around observed trajectory) is standard in prior work (influence functions, TracIn, DVEmb); novelty is primarily in application domain rather than methodology
All experiments use small-to-medium models and dataset subsets; the acknowledged open question about foundation model generalizability severely limits practical impact for modern AI systems

Requires complete, faithfully recorded training history—impractical for many real-world scenarios; no empirical runtime data provided despite O(Kp³) complexity; layer-wise approximation introduces unvalidated independence assumptions

Missing critical experimental validations: no comparison to alternative attribution methods, no ablation studies on design choices, no failure mode analysis, limited guidance on when predictions are unreliable
Most convincing experiments use artificial scenarios (single digit insertion, label corruption); spurious correlation detection validated on only two datasets with single-value outcomes

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Stage-level accountability attribution fills an important gap between data-level and system-level attribution, with clear practical applications for debugging and auditing.

Principled theoretical framework: Rigorous application of potential outcomes formalism with informative error bounds (Theorem 4.1) that characterize when approximations are reliable (late stages, stable regimes, moderate learning rates).

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive experiments across diverse datasets with ground-truth retraining comparisons showing high correlations (0.94-0.98 on multiple benchmarks), plus honest evaluation of failure modes (dispersed backdoors).

Methodological rigor: Taylor approximation properly derived with linearity arguments for multi-step effects; sanity checks validate optimization parameter sensitivity; structured mathematical development from Estimators 4.1-4.3.
Computational efficiency when reused: ET representation computed once during training, then applied to arbitrary test inputs and performance metrics without retraining.
Honest treatment of limitations: Clear discussion of first-order approximation constraints, scalability challenges, exponential error growth for early stages, and batch-level granularity issues.
weaknesses: Fundamental approximation limitation: Exponential error bound e^(2ηΛ(K-min(S))) means early-stage effects are inherently hard to attribute accurately, undermining a key motivation (detecting biases introduced during pretraining). Assumption that trajectories remain close is never empirically verified for deep networks.

Severe scalability constraints: Method requires storing full gradients and optimizer states throughout training; Hessian computation is O(p²); structured approximations (layer-wise, block-wise) are heuristic and unvalidated. Applicability to modern foundation models unclear without significant accuracy loss.
High computational overhead: 3-6× overhead during training for vision tasks; substantial storage costs; this overhead may limit practical adoption despite claims of efficiency.

Limited baseline comparisons: Only DVEmb comparison (adapted from data attribution method); no alternatives from causal inference literature or influence function variants explored. Makes it hard to assess if this is the best approach.
Batch-level granularity limitation: Method loses discriminative power when adversarial signals or biases are dispersed across batches (Figure 7), limiting use for subtle coordinated attacks.
Unverified theoretical assumptions: Theorem 4.1 assumes local stability (∥DΨₖ∥₂ ≤ e^(ηₖΛ)) never empirically confirmed; no investigation of when this fails or how common violations are in practice.

strengths: Well-motivated and timely problem: accountability attribution in multi-stage ML development addresses a real gap in explainability
Sound theoretical framework using potential outcomes formalism with rigorous error bound (Theorem 4.1) characterizing when approximations degrade
Efficient reusable estimators: E_t can be computed once during training and applied to any test input or performance metric
Comprehensive experimental validation with high correlations to retraining-based ground truth (0.94-0.98 on MNIST, 0.53-0.95 on complex datasets)
Honest discussion of limitations including scalability challenges, first-order approximation fragility, and assumptions required
weaknesses: Severe scalability limitations: 3-6× training overhead for logging plus additional attribution cost; authors acknowledge large-scale model applicability remains an open problem, undermining practical utility for foundation models where accountability is most critical

First-order approximation fragility: error bound scales exponentially as e^(2ηΛ(K−min(S))), making early-stage attribution fundamentally unreliable; no empirical characterization of when approximations break down in chaotic training regimes
Limited novelty in estimation method: Taylor expansion and propagator matrix derivations largely replicate influence function techniques; differences from DVEmb are incremental

Experimental validation concerns: largest models tested (Pythia-410M) are small by 2025 standards; high correlation with retraining validates approximation accuracy but not the causal interpretation; spurious correlation experiments limited to two datasets; only DVEmb baseline compared; mostly semi-synthetic experiments

Stage definition ambiguity: insufficient guidance on choosing stage granularity in practice; assumes stages are naturally available but provides no systematic approach for practitioners; treating batches as stages and aggregating fundamentally changes the problem

Questionable counterfactual construction: when skipping stages, learning rate scheduler still advances without observed gradients; multi-stage settings with different data distributions have artificial boundary conditions; consistency assumption under-examined

Limited real-world applicability evidence: no experiments on pretraining→fine-tuning→alignment pipelines (the motivating use case); dispersed backdoor attack shows method loses discriminative power when poisoning spreads across batches, suggesting fundamental batch-level limitations
Error bound provides limited practical guidance: loose bounds depending on unknown constants (Λ, L_γ); practitioners cannot easily assess whether bound is satisfied for their problem

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation addressing an important gap in multi-stage AI system accountability
Principled framework grounded in potential outcomes and causal inference with clear counterfactual semantics
Comprehensive error bound (Theorem 4.1) characterizing when approximation is reliable with insightful dependencies on intervention magnitude, landscape geometry, and time horizon
Accounts for practical optimization dynamics (momentum, learning rate schedules, weight decay) beyond idealized assumptions in prior data attribution work
Efficient estimators with reusable stage representations computed once and applied to any test input or performance function
Extensive experimental validation across vision, NLP, and medical imaging tasks with systematic comparison to retraining ground truth showing 0.94-0.97 correlation
Demonstrates practical utility on spurious correlation detection (CelebA, CivilComments) and adversarial settings (backdoor attacks)
Honest discussion of limitations including scalability challenges, first-order approximation constraints, and trajectory recording overhead without undermining core contributions
Clear presentation with excellent motivation, figures, and detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Scalability limitations: O(p²) space requirements and O(K|B|p²) computation restrict application to small-to-medium models (largest tested: Pythia-410M); structured approximations for scaling are heuristic without theoretical justification

Error bound shows exponential dependence on K-min(S), fundamentally limiting early-stage attribution reliability; no empirical study of approximation error across stages or models to validate bound tightness
Limited baseline comparisons: only DVEmb (adapted to stages) with competitive but close results (0.9456 vs 0.9417); missing comparisons to simpler alternatives or other causal inference approaches
Stage granularity choice remains user-dependent; limited practical guidance on selecting stage boundaries without natural separation, though acknowledged in Section 6
Narrow scope of performance functions: experiments focus on log-likelihood; claims about reusability for any performance function not thoroughly validated

Trajectory recording overhead significant (1.1-6× depending on model) and only partially mitigated by structured approximations; storage burden for large-scale practice

First-order approximation may miss significant higher-order effects, especially in chaotic training regimes; assumptions on Lipschitz Hessian continuity and local stability validity in practice not discussed
